title: Custom
hookLine: a community's custom can carry the weight of law
last: HALAKHA IS A PATH, WALKED STEP BY STEP.

cards: It's the morning before Passover in two neighboring towns. In one, the shops are open and the workshops busy until noon, the way they always are. In the next town over, people have put their tools down.
Same holiday, same Torah, different mornings. Now a carpenter from the first town walks into the second, ready to work. Is he doing something wrong?
Is the second town too strict? The Mishnah takes up this very case, and its answer doesn't come from a verse. It comes from what each town does.

teach.b: Minhag. It's the Hebrew word for custom, the practice a community has taken on, and in Jewish law it can carry real weight. First, the Mishnah, in tractate Pesachim.
Where people are accustomed to work on the eve of Passover until midday, they work. Where they're accustomed not to, they don't. The place decides.
Second, the traveler. Someone who goes from one kind of place to the other, the Mishnah says, takes on the stricter practice of both the place he left and the place he's in.

teach.h: DON'T STAND OUT AGAINST THE TOWN.
teach.b: And it adds a reason that's not about rules at all: a person shouldn't stand out against local custom, because of the quarrels it can cause. Custom keeps the peace of a community. Third, custom can outlast its reason.
The Talmud, in tractate Beitzah, tells of Jews outside the land of Israel who kept an extra festival day, because long ago they couldn't be sure of the calendar in time. Later the calendar was known.
Should they drop the extra day?

teach.h: YOUR ANCESTORS' CUSTOM IN YOUR HANDS.
teach.b: The answer sent to them: be careful with the custom of your ancestors that is in your hands.

teach.h: A FAMILY IS A COMMUNITY TOO.
teach.b: Fourth, a family is a community too.
One family keeps a dish for one holiday, another lights candles a certain way, a third sings a tune nobody else knows. The law leaves room for these, and communities hold them as their own.
A path walked by your grandparents isn't nothing.

how: Jewish communities keep their own customs in prayer, food and holidays, and families pass down their minhagim. Ashkenazi and Sephardi communities, for example, follow different customs on a number of practices, and communities often treat their own as binding for themselves.

o: a custom a community takes on, with real weight
a habit that has no place in Jewish law
a rule the Torah gives to every single town

p: work until midday, or don't: the place decides
takes on the stricter of both places

s: Jewish law decides everything by verses alone, never by custom
in Pesachim, whether to work on the eve of Passover depends on the town's custom.
the Mishnah warns against standing out from local custom
because of the quarrels it can cause.
once the calendar was known, the Talmud told communities to drop the extra festival day
the answer was to keep the custom of their ancestors that was in their hands.

games.q: you're a carpenter from a town that works on the eve of Passover. you've just arrived in a town where everyone rests. what do you do?
o: work; your hometown's custom goes with you.
rest; take on the stricter practice and don't stand out.
ask for a vote of the town.
games.why: the Mishnah puts the stricter practice of both places on the traveler, and warns against standing out because of the quarrels it causes.

practice: Bring to mind one thing your family does, or did, a certain way, religious or not: a dish on a certain day, a word said at the door, the way birthdays went. Who taught it to whom?
Hold it for a few breaths, the way you'd hold something handed down, with the people in it.

wordCard.voice: Minhag. Custom: the practice a community or family has taken on, which Jewish law treats with real weight. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: custom. The plural is minhagim. Ashkenazi pronunciation: MIN-hahg.

carryVoice: Your line: custom is law too. A town's way of doing things is part of its peace. I'll be here tomorrow.
